title: Γέρων καὶ θάνατος
part: The Old Man and Death (Chambry 78 · Perry 60)
source: Émile Chambry, Ésope: Fables, texte établi et traduit (Les Belles Lettres, Paris, 1927), fable 78 (= Perry 60). Text as printed, including Chambry's editorial punctuation (« », [ ] for words Chambry deletes as interpolated). Pronunciation: reconstructed Attic, after W. S. Allen, Vox Graeca. Romanization: standard classical transliteration (ē/ō; th/ph/ch; y for υ, u in diphthongs; h = rough breathing; ēi/āi/ōi for iota subscript; accents omitted).

sentences.t: Γέρων ποτὲ ξύλα κόψας καὶ ταῦτα φέρων πολλὴν ὁδὸν ἐβάδιζε.
sentences.tr: Gerōn pote xyla kopsas kai tauta pherōn pollēn hodon ebadize.
sentences.l: An old man, having once cut wood and carrying it, was walking a long road.
sentences.i: An old man had cut wood one day, and was walking a long way with it.
sentences.n: The fable's engine, visible in the first line: an aorist participle (κόψας) names the act already finished, a present participle (φέρων) the action going on alongside the main verb. πολλὴν ὁδόν is the accusative of extent of space — not what he walked to, but how far.

sentences.t: Διὰ δὲ τὸν κόπον τῆς ὁδοῦ ἀποθέμενος τὸ φορτίον τὸν Θάνατον ἐπεκαλεῖτο.
sentences.tr: Dia de ton kopon tēs hodou apothemenos to phortion ton Thanaton epekaleito.
sentences.l: And because of the toil of the road, having set down the burden, he called upon Death.
sentences.i: Worn out by the journey, he set his load down and began calling on Death.
sentences.n: κόπος is at once the labour and the exhaustion it leaves behind. ἀποθέμενος is middle: he put the load off himself. The imperfect ἐπεκαλεῖτο is not one shout but a calling that goes on — which is why Death has time to arrive. Θάνατος is written with a capital because he is a person here, and can be summoned.

sentences.t: Τοῦ δὲ Θανάτου φανέντος καὶ πυθομένου δι᾽ ἣν αἰτίαν αὐτὸν παρακαλεῖται, ὁ γέρων ἔφη· « Ἵνα τὸ φορτίον ἄρῃς. »
sentences.tr: Tou de Thanatou phanentos kai pythomenou di’ hēn aitian auton parakaleitai, ho gerōn ephē· « Hina to phortion arēis. »
sentences.l: And Death having appeared and having enquired for what reason he was calling him, the old man said: « So that you may lift the burden. »
sentences.i: When Death appeared and asked what he was calling him for, the old man said: « To lift my load. »
sentences.n: A genitive absolute carrying two participles at once (φανέντος καὶ πυθομένου). παρακαλεῖται is middle — the old man calls Death to himself — and it stays present, because Greek keeps the tense of the question actually asked where English shifts it into the past. The answer is a bare purpose clause, ἵνα with the aorist subjunctive ἄρῃς, standing alone: the whole reply is the 'why'.

sentences.t: Ὁ μῦθος δηλοῖ ὅτι πᾶς ἄνθρωπος φιλόζωος, [ἐν τῷ βίῳ] κἂν δυστυχῇ.
sentences.tr: Ho mythos dēloi hoti pas anthrōpos philozōos, [en tōi biōi] kan dystychēi.
sentences.l: The fable shows that every man is life-loving, [in life] even if he fares badly.
sentences.i: The fable shows that every man clings to life, [in life] even if things go badly for him.
sentences.n: Square brackets mark words Chambry judges an interpolation and deletes — here a limp 'in life' after φιλόζωος has already said it. κἄν is καὶ ἐάν run together by crasis, with the subjunctive δυστυχῇ.
